feral

FEER-uhl -- shares a root with 'ferocious.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Feral is wild and untamed, especially after having lived in captivity or domestication.

A pack of feral cats had taken over the abandoned warehouse, with no owner in sight.

Example

A dog that escaped its backyard years ago now avoids every human it sees, hunting its own food and sleeping under a highway overpass instead of a porch.

That return to a wild, untamed state after once being domesticated is exactly what feral describes. Unlike 'wild,' which can describe any animal never tamed, feral specifically implies going wild after domestication.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wild: Wild describes any animal living in its natural state -- one that has never been tamed by anyone at all. Feral is narrower: a feral animal, or its recent ancestors, once lived with humans and has since returned to the wild without human care.

stray: A stray is a pet that is lost or has no owner right now, but it still lives among people and may approach them. A feral animal has gone further -- it has returned fully to the wild and avoids humans altogether.

skittish: Skittish means easily startled and jumpy -- even a well-kept stable horse can be skittish in a storm. Feral is not about nerves; it means a once-domesticated animal now lives wild, entirely outside human care.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

domesticated: tamed and adapted to living with humans

tame: gentle and not dangerous; accustomed to humans

Where it sits · how fierce and dangerous it turns — untamed → feral → savage

untamed vs. feral: Untamed is milder than feral on this scale -- untamed says only that no human controls the animal, while feral adds the wary, sometimes aggressive edge of a creature that has gone back to the wild after domestication.

savage vs. feral: Savage can feel more intense than feral: feral emphasizes a return to an untamed state, while savage adds a sense of fierce, sometimes violent aggression on top of that wildness.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -fer-

root — -fer-: wild (Latin (ferus))

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: relating to, characteristic of (Latin (-alis))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ferus meant 'wild, untamed,' and the adjective ending -al ('characteristic of') completes the word -- feral describes a creature that has gone back to that wild state. The same root gives us ferocious.

Use the root in a new word: ferocious

Use the root in a new word: ferocious: The nature documentary captured a ferocious battle between two rival wolf packs.
